title: Arithmetic Slices II - Subsequence
statement:
Count how many subsequences of the integer array `nums` are arithmetic, and return that count.

- A subsequence keeps some of the elements (possibly all of them) in their original order; two subsequences are different when they use different sets of positions, even if their values match.
- A sequence is arithmetic when it has three or more elements and every element minus the one before it gives the same difference (which may be zero or negative).

The inputs guarantee that the count fits in a signed 32-bit integer.
constraints: The answer fits in a signed 32-bit integer
notes:
## Intuition

Listing every subsequence costs O(2^n). Instead, notice that an arithmetic subsequence is fixed by its last element and its common difference: extending one that ends at index `j` with difference `d` by an element `nums[i]` works exactly when `nums[i] - nums[j] = d`. So for every index keep a hash map from difference to how many runs end there. The trick is to also count runs of length 2 (any pair is a valid start); a pair becomes a real (length 3+) subsequence only once something extends it.

## Approach

1. Give each index `i` a map `dp[i]`: difference → number of runs of length at least 2 that end at `i` with that difference.
2. For every pair `j < i`, compute `diff = nums[i] - nums[j]`.
3. `before = dp[j].get(diff)` runs end at `j` with that difference. Appending `nums[i]` to each gives a run of length at least 3, so add `before` to `total`.
4. Store `before + 1` more runs in `dp[i][diff]`: the extended ones plus the new pair `(j, i)`.
5. Return `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]`, so every pair differs by 2, 4, 6 or 8.

- `i = 1`: the pair (2, 4) gives `dp[1] = {2: 1}`.
- `i = 2`: `diff = 2` with `j = 1` finds `before = 1`, so `total = 1` ([2, 4, 6]) and `dp[2][2] = 2`.
- `i = 3`: `diff = 2` with `j = 2` finds `before = 2`, so `total = 3` and `dp[3][2] = 3`.
- `i = 4`: `diff = 4` with `j = 2` finds 1 ([2, 6, 10]), and `diff = 2` with `j = 3` finds 3, so `total = 7`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): one constant-time map update per pair.
- Space: O(n²): each map can hold up to n differences.

## Pitfalls

- Differences can reach 2^32 - 1 in size; in Java or C compute them in 64 bits, or `0 - (-2^31)` and `-2^31 - 0` look equal.
- Add `before`, not `before + 1`, to `total`: the extra 1 is a bare pair, which is too short to count.
- Equal values must still be counted separately; `[7, 7, 7, 7, 7]` has 16 answers, not 3.
- Read `dp[j]` before updating `dp[i]`; for `j < i` they are different maps, so the order inside the loop is safe.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp[i]` | map from difference to the number of runs (length ≥ 2) ending at index `i` |
| `i`, `j` | the new last element and the element just before it |
| `diff` | `nums[i] - nums[j]`, the step of the run being extended |
| `before` | how many runs with that step already end at `j` |
| `total` | arithmetic subsequences of length at least 3 found so far |

narration.3: One map per index: difference to the number of runs of length 2 or more ending there.
narration.4: The count of arithmetic subsequences with at least three elements.
narration.5: Choose the index i that will be the last element.
narration.6: Choose the element j just before it.
narration.7: The step a run must have for nums[i] to follow nums[j].
narration.8: How many runs with that step already end at j.
narration.9: Each of them plus nums[i] has at least three elements, so they all count.
narration.10: Those extended runs and the new pair (j, i) now end at i with this step.
narration.13: Every pair was processed; return the count.
